rationale: Global equity, accumulating, physical, very large and cheap. Every preference in the profile is met and the only gap is the realised tracking difference, which is not a critical field. This is the shape the policy is meant to reward.
Developed-world core holding at twelve basis points. Slightly narrower than a full all-world fund but cheaper, so it should land in the same band.
The same strategy as VWCE in a distributing share class. The accumulating preference is unmet, which must cost points without disqualifying an otherwise excellent fund.
Cheapest band and enormous scale, held back by a 36% top-ten weight and a single-market mandate. Should still clear the shortlist threshold but by a smaller margin than a global fund.

The cheapest S&P 500 exposure in the snapshot, penalised twice for being swap-based: once on fund structure, once on the stated physical-replication preference. The gap to CSPX is the price of the structure.
Near-perfect diversification at a higher cost and a shorter record. Deliberately included as a boundary case near the research/shortlist threshold.
Broad emerging-market exposure is a legitimate candidate for a high risk tolerance over twenty years. The region penalty and the unmet breadth preference cost it, but neither disqualifies it.
A long-established, liquid fund whose index holds 101 names with half the weight in ten of them. Concentration and the distributing share class pull it out of shortlist territory.
A sound single-market fund that fits the profile poorly: distributing, regionally narrow, and modest in size. Research rather than shortlist.

A large, cheap, well-diversified euro corporate bond fund. Its standalone quality is high and its fit with a twenty-year, high-risk-tolerance mandate is not, so the profile-fit cap must stop it shortlisting on quality alone. This is the distinction the whole project exists to draw.

The issuer does not publish a top-ten concentration figure for a ten-thousand-holding index. Renormalising over the remaining weight flatters the fund, which is exactly why an incomplete record cannot reach shortlist.

Very short-dated Treasury bills: cheap and liquid, but twenty holdings and a cash-substitute role for a growth mandate. Low diversification and poor asset-class fit, with a missing concentration figure on top.
A narrow theme whose size and concentration were not verified for this snapshot. Two critical metrics are absent, so the record cannot support a shortlist however the remaining weight scores.
A long-established theme fund at 65 basis points with a hundred holdings and a 45% top-ten weight. Expensive and concentrated, but broad enough geographically and old enough not to reject.

The most expensive, most concentrated and most narrowly focused fund in the snapshot, and swap-based on top. It fails on cost, diversification and fit simultaneously, which is what the reject band is for. No hard constraint is involved: the score alone rejects it.

Whole-of-market United States equity at three basis points: the highest score of any rejected fund in the snapshot, and second only to IWDA-AMS overall. The profile requires UCITS eligibility and this fund is United States domiciled, so it is rejected outright. The score is published anyway, because a rejection nobody can explain is not auditable.
The oldest and largest exchange-traded fund in the world is still not investable under a profile that requires UCITS. Age and scale cannot lift a hard constraint.
A single-asset commodity trust: no diversification, poor asset-class fit for a growth mandate, and non-UCITS. Two independent reasons to reject, and the hard constraint is the one that decides.

The Xetra listing of the same Irish fund as VUSA-LSE, sharing its ticker and ISIN. Both listings must evaluate identically, and only etf_id may distinguish them; anything keyed on ticker alone is a defect.
The London listing of the same fund as VUSA-XETRA. Paired with it deliberately so a divergence between two listings of one fund fails a test.
